analysis.one_liner: Overhauls the Superfund toxic-cleanup law to limit polluters' liability, speed up cleanups, and reinstate its industry taxes for five years.
analysis.headline: The Superfund Reform Act drew 45 cosponsors from both parties and held two subcommittee hearings, but the House never voted on it; the action record points instead to a separate Superfund bill, and the measure expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program makes polluters pay to clean up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. This bill would rewrite the program: companies that sent waste to a site before 1987, municipal dump users, small-quantity disposers, recyclers, railroads, and pipeline holders would largely be exempt from cleanup liability, municipalities would have their share capped, and lawsuits between responsible parties would be restricted. Cleanups would have to be 'cost-effective' and tailored to how the land will actually be used, and limits would be placed on damages the public can collect for destroyed natural resources. The bill also carries genuine community-participation and brownfield-redevelopment provisions, and it would reinstate the Superfund taxes on chemical and petroleum companies through 2002, raising the collection cap from $11.97 billion to $22 billion.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that generated or transported hazardous waste to contaminated sites would gain the most, since much of their liability for old sites would be wiped out or capped. Municipalities, small businesses, scrap and battery recyclers, and developers of contaminated 'brownfield' land would also gain protection. Communities near sites would gain new rights to participate in cleanup decisions and get help redeveloping brownfields, though the cleanups themselves could be less thorough.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts from Superfund liability companies whose last waste-disposal activity occurred before 1987, parties whose waste was only municipal trash or sewage sludge, and small-quantity disposers, unless it is shown they contributed significantly to the contamination or obstructed cleanup [S2].

Exempts or limits liability for scrap, paper, and battery recyclers, railroads with short spur tracks, pipeline right-of-way holders, construction contractors, and innocent heirs to contaminated land, and caps municipalities' share of landfill cleanup costs [S2].

Restricts lawsuits among responsible parties, puts litigation on hold while a neutral allocator divides up responsibility at multi-party sites, and requires parties who sue improperly to pay the other side's defense costs [S2].
Requires cleanup remedies to be cost-effective and based on how land and water will actually be used, and sets an acceptable lifetime cancer-risk range of one in 10,000 to one in 1,000,000 [S2].

Limits what the public can recover for damaged natural resources: it bars payment for 'non-use' value, bars the contingent-valuation method of pricing lost resources, and bars recovery for damage that occurred before December 1980 [S2].

Lets states with voluntary cleanup programs handle contaminated sites largely free of federal Superfund enforcement, lets the EPA delegate authority to states, and requires a governor's concurrence before a new site is added to the national priorities list [S2].

Adds community-participation rights, community assistance groups, and technical assistance grants, makes federal facilities fully subject to cleanup requirements, and authorizes public-health assistance for affected communities, including Indian tribes [S2].
Reinstates Superfund taxes on chemical feedstocks and related sources through 2002 and raises the amount that may be collected from $11.97 billion to $22 billion [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the compliant part of industry would bear the cost: where polluters are exempted, the Superfund itself picks up their share of cleanup costs, which the bill refills by extending taxes on chemical and petroleum interests. Residents near toxic sites could face less thorough cleanups, since remedies would be tailored to anticipated land use, and the public would collect less for damaged natural resources.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near waste sites

drawbacks.text: Liability exemptions shift cleanup costs onto the Superfund itself, which the bill refills by raising the tax cap to $22 billion — meaning taxpayers and compliant companies pay for contamination the original polluters would otherwise have funded [S2].

Directing remedies toward 'current and reasonably anticipated uses' of land and deferring to state determinations on groundwater could leave contamination in place at sites planned for commercial rather than residential reuse, and weaker groundwater sources could be written off [S2].

The natural resource damages title bars recovery for lost non-use values and for injuries occurring before December 1980, reducing what the public can collect when rivers, groundwater, or habitats are destroyed [S2].

Delegating authority to states and requiring a governor's concurrence to list new sites could slow or weaken federal cleanup enforcement, though the bill lets EPA deny state funding where state standards are more stringent than federal ones [S2].
The cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: the five-year tax extension raises costs on chemical and petroleum manufacturers, costs that can be passed to consumers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles real improvements — community participation rights, brownfield liability protection, health assistance for affected communities, and a funding extension — with a broad rollback of polluter liability and cost-driven cleanup standards. Weighing them honestly, the liability exemptions and the tightened natural-resource-damage rules are the heart of the bill, and they move cleanup costs from the companies that created the contamination to the Superfund and the public. The community and brownfield provisions are genuine, but they ride along on a bill whose main effect is to make old-site cleanup cheaper for polluting industries. In the event, none of it mattered: the bill never received a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and its subcommittee held hearings, but nothing was ever approved, and in June 1998 the action record simply points to a separate Superfund bill; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Oxley introduced the Superfund Reform Act on November 9, 1997, with a large bipartisan list of original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The Speaker assigned it to three committees at once — Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Ways and Means — splitting its provisions among them [S5].
It finished with 45 cosponsors: 21 Democrats and 24 Republicans [S4].
Subcommittees in Commerce and Transportation held hearings in March 1998, but neither committee ever voted to send the bill to the floor [S5].

On June 22, 1998, the action record says only 'See H.R. 2727,' pointing to a separate Superfund bill, and no further action was taken on H.R. 3000 before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, companies facing Superfund liability for old waste sites kept the current rules and the public kept today's cleanup standards. But the bill's community-participation, brownfield, and funding provisions died with it, and the Superfund taxes that lapsed in 1995 were not reinstated — so in the short run, polluting industries that would have paid those taxes also came out ahead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities kept current cleanup standards; no reform passed

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — 21 of its 45 cosponsors were Democrats and 24 were Republicans — and the record shows no party-line vote, because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Industrial waste generators and transporters (chemical manufacturers, refiners, shippers)
industries.note: The bill would exempt companies whose waste shipments to a site ended before 1987, restrict contribution lawsuits among them, and cap recoverable costs. The mechanism matters for ordinary people: cleanup money those companies would otherwise pay would come from the Superfund instead, which the bill refills with taxes reaching $22 billion.

The bill deems recycling transactions exempt from liability if the material met commercial specifications and the recycler used reasonable care — encouraging recycling while removing legal accountability when recycled materials end up contaminating a site.

industries.industry: Brownfield developers and real estate interests
industries.note: Liability protection for prospective buyers, contiguous owners, and participants in state voluntary cleanup programs would make redeveloping contaminated land far cheaper — a benefit that can reach communities through redevelopment, but paired with state-run cleanups largely outside federal enforcement.
Small and large municipalities get their landfill liability capped, and small-quantity disposers are exempt — shifting those costs to the Superfund and, ultimately, taxpayers.

The same companies that gain liability relief would pay reinstated Superfund excise taxes through 2002 under a doubled $22 billion collection cap — though those costs can be passed through to consumers.
The bill shields existing indemnification and insurance contracts from the new liability rules and limits claims, reducing long-tail Superfund exposure for insurers.
